reason: The sources provide multi-site verified details of the landmark 2017 neutron star collision, its gravitational waves, and the cosmic forging of heavy elements.
story: On August 17, 2017, observatories on Earth detected gravitational waves rippling across spacetime from two colliding neutron stars over 130 million light-years away in the galaxy NGC 4993. Seconds later, a burst of gamma rays erupted, followed by an expanding fireball known as a kilonova. Merging neutron stars create an extreme surge of free neutrons that drives the rapid neutron-capture process, synthesizing elements heavier than iron that standard stellar cores cannot produce. The radioactive decay of these newly minted heavy elements, including gold and uranium, generated a brilliant glowing flash roughly a thousand times brighter than a classical nova. Remarkably, spectral observations revealed that the early expanding fireball of debris was nearly perfectly spherical. This single catastrophic crash definitively confirmed that the universe's heaviest and most precious metals are forged in the cataclysmic wreckage of dead stars.
angle: The collision of two city-sized dead stars produces a cataclysmic kilonova explosion that ripples spacetime and forges cosmic supplies of heavy metals like gold and uranium.

claims.claim: Neutron stars are the ultra-dense collapsed remnants left behind when massive stars explode as supernovae.
When two orbiting neutron stars spiral together and merge, they emit ripples in spacetime known as gravitational waves.
The collision of neutron stars produces an explosive optical and infrared transient known as a kilonova.
A kilonova's peak brightness reaches roughly 1,000 times that of a classical nova.
On August 17, 2017, the gravitational wave signal GW170817 from a binary neutron star merger was detected by LIGO and Virgo.
GW170817 was pinpointed to the galaxy NGC 4993, located more than 130 million light-years from Earth.
GW170817 was accompanied by a short gamma-ray burst detected almost immediately after the gravitational wave signal.
GW170817/AT2017gfo was the first unambiguously confirmed observation of a kilonova.
Neutron star collisions create an intense neutron flux that drives the rapid neutron-capture process (r-process).
The r-process in neutron star mergers forges heavy elements such as gold and uranium that cannot form in normal stars.
Heavy elements formed in a kilonova block blue light while allowing red light to escape, causing the explosion to glow with a distinct red color.
Spectral analysis of the AT2017gfo kilonova definitively identified the heavy element strontium in the debris.
Spectral modeling demonstrated that the early expanding fireball of the AT2017gfo kilonova was highly spherical.
A neutron star merger remnant collapses into either a more massive neutron star or a black hole.
Astronomers propose using spherical kilonova explosions as standard candles to measure the rate of cosmic expansion and address the Hubble tension.
In August 2025, LIGO and Virgo detected signal S250818k, indicating a merger involving at least one object less massive than the Sun.
The candidate optical counterpart AT2025ulz initially resembled a kilonova before shifting into a stripped-envelope supernova.

disputed: Distance to NGC 4993: Sources S1 and S2 specify 140 million light-years, whereas S7 states 130 million light-years. Scripts should state 'between 130 and 140 million light-years away'.

Nature of AT2025ulz: Sources S4 and S6 note that scientists are divided on whether AT2025ulz represents a true 'superkilonova' or a chance alignment with an unrelated supernova. Scripts should attribute this as an unresolved candidate hypothesis.

Candidate versus confirmed kilonova count: S1 and S2 list several gamma-ray burst candidate events like GRB 130603B and GRB 211211A, while S4 and S6 maintain that only GW170817 is unambiguously confirmed. Scripts should clarify that GW170817 remains the single definitively confirmed event.
